tweets.text:
Some meta level observations:

1) Dario’s tweets benefit from scarcity. The fact that he doesn’t “spend much time” on X makes a tweet carry more weight and is itself a statement of seriousness

2) He (and Sholto) selected the right person to engage with. Gavin is an ideal steelman; he’s a legit critic but is civil and well informed. Having him as the interlocutor makes everyone look better and makes for a stronger debate

3) Going direct with a personal post was the escalation after a senior colleague (ie Sholto) already did the fact checking and elevated the debate to the level of principles. So Dario was able to come in and focus on his beliefs rather than having to first debate the details of who said what when

4) The personal post was actually personal. Parts like the story about his father make it less likely to read like PR ghostwriting, and thus give it more power. The personal story also makes the post more memorable because it’s specific and concrete and relatable 

5) The argument in part 2 is an interesting insight into how he assesses his own messaging. When accused of negative messaging (qualitative), he rebuts that it’s roughly balanced in large part because he’s written one essay about benefits and one about risks (quantitative). Implication: he’s taking an analytical approach to measuring positivity, but many others are simply going off vibes - so this won’t be the last time he and his critics talk past each other

"Small-Scale Experiments: Are We There Yet?"

Scaling laws show up even in tiny 4M parameter models, but only when their hyperparameters are tuned well enough.

This Meta paper found that small models are much more hyperparameter-sensitive. As scale increases, the hyperparameter loss surface becomes lower-dimensional, eventually approaching one effective tuning direction.

So the scaling gap may be less about small models failing to predict large ones, and more about under-tuning them.

https://t.co/WIK2E0xWbV

"Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding"

Across 1,867 repos, CLAUDE.md-style files grow +226% because adding instructions is cheap, but deleting them gets riskier as their rationale is forgotten.

The older an instruction gets, the less likely anyone is to delete it because the reason it was added is increasingly hard to recover.

Their fix is simple: save why each instruction was added, so future maintainers know when it is safe to remove.

That let them eliminate 99.3% of unnecessary instructions and improve real-world instruction-following by up to 23.1%.

https://t.co/bTRQ65EAep

"Dion3: Full-Stack Orthogonal Updates"

Dion3 makes Muon practical at scale.

Instead of running Newton-Schulz on the full momentum matrix, it orthogonalizes a selected row subset, reformulates the iteration over the smaller Gram matrix, exploits symmetry with custom CuteDSL GEMMs, and megabatches distributed communication.

At 25% row selection, it reaches equal or better loss than NorMuon while cutting optimizer-step time by up to 6.5x

https://t.co/dZjNNBlInZ

tweets.text:
Amazing outcome. Cursor executed the applied AI strategy flawlessly. 

Most people completely underestimated the market size in AI coding. The biggest developer tool exits in history were on the order of low billions of dollars. And it was already assumed to be a heavily competitive and somewhat saturated space when they really got going.

Multiple mental models shattered near instantly. The market sizes for agentic coding was far larger than most realized. There was actually tons and tons of room to innovate between the user and the underlying model, and even on the model itself.

Cursor provided out the applied AI playbook by figuring out the right product shape for agentic coding work, acting as a neutral layer between models and the workflows, post training models for the areas that make most sense to drive down costs or improve performance, building out the right infra stack for the relevant workflows, building out a strong category-aligned GTM motion, and more.

Great set of lessons for anyone doing applied AI right now. We’re going to see a lot more of these.

They’re lamenting about how how some of the critical contracts and partnerships that would give them credibility (and revenue and network effects) are basically stuck at the 1-yard line. This is a massively fragmented market. And this is btw just straight up pure bureaucracy. The champions, terms and everything is lined up. It’s purely a win win situation but summer and one random clause is the issue. And, it might cause them to not reach their ambitious timelines. 

And I’m sitting there smiling and eventually laughing and at some point they ask what’s funny. I tell them “do you know how long it’ll take anyone to do the same thing as you” - and this is with leverage and relationships that they already have. 

And, this in the short term is painful but in the long term becomes such a strong moat. That they’ll look back and laugh why they were worried about a few days when in the long term this is what will make them one of the biggest companies in the world. 

Unnecessary and 996 performative pain is not the moat. But building entrenched software and relationships that take a lot of pain is a moat :)

tweets.text:
The Gavin Baker vs. Sholto Douglas exchange on the economic concentration of power of AI is one of the best AI debates. Here's a gist with some context and some thoughts:

One of the central themes of the debate offense-defense balance and how it governs whether AI is (or should be) concentrated in the hands of few or distributed to many.

The core idea behind offense-defense balance, outlined in Robert Jervis's 1978 essay "Cooperation Under the Security Dilemma" on world politics, is: for a given technology, is it cheaper to attack or to defend?

Baker initially argues that he agrees with Zuck's view in his essay that AI should be distributed and not concentrated into a few corporations' hands. Sholto rebuts that it squarely depends on the offense-defense balance of the domain (cyber, bio, etc). And even if you do distribute, the bottleneck is compute.

He cites two domains:
— Cyber he says is defense-dominant, eventually. If it's opened up today, the cost to attack is minimal and the you cannot defend quickly enough. We'll need a ~2yrs of hardening the critical systems like financial institutions and infra providers before this may no longer be a risk.

— Bio he says is offense-dominant well into the 2030s. Synthesizing deadly self-replicating pathogens could cost O($10K) and vaccines cost billions and years. You just can't patch the human body with smarter models.

The distribute everything vs gate everything is a false dichotomy. You want to distribute in defense dominant domains and gate in offense dominant. And its all extra muddied because capabilities are dependent on compute which is extremely unequally distributed. And compute eventually dictates proliferation of capabilities.
______________

Both gloss over some offense dominant domains that are already distributed massively: 

— Propaganda and persuasion, for example, were once regarded offense dominant yet already ubiquitous today. That said, technology changes, and watermarking outputs and AI detection tools may have shifted it to being defense dominant. 

— Mass surveillance is also offense dominant (usually the attacker is the state) and most LLMs you can use for <$1/M toks can do this today. Today, even non-state actors (private cos) can surveil you in pretty dangerous detail by running agent swarms on vast amounts of public data.

Both Gavin and Sholto are right, and we see it today.
— Sholto's right: the very pinnacle of frontier capabilities is locked away in those who have compute and will continue to be. The shape of compute of the >100 GW compute by 2030 is almost known at this point. Between 6-7 US entities (2 big labs, 3 hyperscalers clouds, Meta/xAI) will own or control 65-75%. With RSI around the corner, as long as it holds true that more compute leads to being able to train and serve more powerful models at scale, those companies will have proprietary frontier capabilities and only they / the market will dictate when they need to release them. Notably, this isn't monopolistic concentration of power since multiple parties will have that capability.

— Gavin's right too: frontier capabilities in certain domains are making it to the public and will continue to do so. Models are getting cheaper. Whether we like it or not, people can do dangerous things with models today. LLMs already cyber exploits that are less talked about (take even the LLM-assisted hack on the nationwide Indian exam system, CBSE). As long as prices for models continue to fall at a more rapid rate (10x YoY) than growth in compute (2-3x YoY), this dynamic will continue. Frontier intelligence will continue to be more accessible.

This is a beautiful homage to the young Indias, all under 27, building difficult hard tech, who decided their dreams don’t need to ask for permission.

— Ahmad Faraaz (26) & Harshit Awasthi (26), Kalam Labs: stratospheric UAVs, near-space aerial vehicles for military surveillance
— Aadit Palicha (24) & Kaivalya Vohra (23), Zepto: 10-minute grocery delivery
— Khushi Mittal (22), Aspera: autonomous amphibious cargo aircraft for long-range aerial logistics
— Samay Sanghvi (19), Alteon: dynamic-soaring UAVs that can stay aloft ~417 days for maritime surveillance
— Angad Daryani (27), Praan: next-gen air purifiers
— Naman Pushp (21), Airbound: tail-sitter delivery drones targeting one-cent deliveries
— Shreepoorna Rao (23), Arctus: high-altitude, long-endurance UAVs for earth observation cheaper than satellites

Even ~10yrs ago, there were few examples you could look up to to take such a big leap of faith. Now, there are tons. Incredibly inspiring for the next generation.

The kids are alright.
